claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with celiac disease confirmed in the scoped pathway.

claims.statement: Starting gluten avoidance before diagnostic testing can alter serologic and biopsy results.
claims.limitation: The content does not prescribe a gluten challenge.
claims.applicablePopulation: People undergoing evaluation for possible celiac disease.

claims.statement: IgG-based celiac serology has a limited diagnostic role when IgA deficiency makes IgA-based tests unreliable.
claims.limitation: This does not make an IgG panel the preferred routine first test before total IgA context is known.
claims.applicablePopulation: People evaluated for celiac disease when IgA deficiency is present or suspected.

claims.statement: HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 typing addresses genetic susceptibility and does not by itself establish active celiac disease.
claims.limitation: This claim does not specify test performance or every clinical use of HLA typing.
claims.applicablePopulation: People undergoing evaluation for possible celiac disease.

claims.statement: A positive screening FIT requires diagnostic colonoscopy; FIT alone does not diagnose colorectal cancer.
claims.limitation: Suitability and the management of incomplete examination remain individualized.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a positive colorectal-cancer screening FIT who are suitable for outpatient diagnostic evaluation.

claims.statement: Histologic examination of tissue sampled from a suspicious colorectal lesion provides confirming evidence of cancer.
claims.limitation: Gross appearance and cross-sectional imaging can be suspicious but do not substitute for tissue diagnosis or assign stage here.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a suspicious colorectal lesion sampled during colonoscopy.

claims.statement: Iron studies are used to confirm iron deficiency in an already anemic patient, and low ferritin supports depleted iron stores.
claims.limitation: A normal ferritin can be misleading with inflammation; this content uses no numeric threshold and does not claim isolated low ferritin proves anemia.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with established anemia undergoing evaluation for iron deficiency.

claims.statement: New unexplained confirmed iron-deficiency anemia in adult men or postmenopausal patients generally warrants gastrointestinal evaluation with upper endoscopy and colonoscopy when suitable.
claims.limitation: Suitability, individual context, and alternative established causes must be considered; no referral deadline is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adult men and explicitly postmenopausal patients with newly confirmed otherwise unexplained iron-deficiency anemia.

claims.statement: MRI is appropriate for local characterization of a deep, enlarging, or ultrasound-indeterminate extremity soft-tissue mass before biopsy.
claims.limitation: MRI can characterize and guide planning but cannot by itself prove sarcoma.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with a deep, enlarging, or ultrasound-indeterminate extremity soft-tissue mass.

claims.statement: A suspicious extremity soft-tissue mass should reach an experienced sarcoma team before a planned image-guided core biopsy so the biopsy path respects a future surgical approach.
claims.limitation: Biopsy technique and selected incisional approaches remain specialist decisions; imaging suspicion is not a tissue diagnosis.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults whose extremity mass remains suspicious after local MRI characterization.

claims.statement: Rectus diastasis is widening of the midline connective tissue between the rectus muscles.
claims.limitation: EHS KQ1 and current NHS leaflet. No numerical separation cutoff, demographic probability or treatment rule is used; EHS describes limited evidence.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with supplied abdominal-wall examination findings.

claims.statement: Rectus separation can produce a broad midline dome when the abdominal wall is engaged.
claims.limitation: Current NHS leaflet is the sole direct source for the dome description. A clinical pattern, not a pathognomonic sign or proof from appearance alone.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with broad midline doming during a supplied examination.

claims.statement: Clinical examination is generally sufficient to identify rectus diastasis.
claims.limitation: EHS KQ2, low-quality evidence. Imaging may be useful when another question, including a coexisting hernia, needs assessment. These recognition cases do not establish a universal no-imaging rule.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing clinical assessment of rectus separation.

claims.statement: A focal abdominal-wall hernia involves protrusion through a gap or weak area rather than rectus separation alone.
claims.limitation: Independent synthesis of NHS hernia definition and EHS diastasis definition/coexisting-hernia discussion. The two can coexist; the supplied examination identifies no focal defect. No assertion that examination excludes all hernias.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults distinguishing a supplied separation pattern from a focal hernia.

claims.statement: An epidermoid cyst often presents as a slowly growing cutaneous lump with a central punctum.
claims.limitation: Hoang clinical/pathophysiology sections plus broad NHS skin-cyst corroboration. Presumptive recognition, not histologic confirmation. The NHS displayed review date is 2023 with an overdue 2026 review marker.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with an uncomplicated slowly enlarging skin lump.

claims.statement: A central punctum supports epidermoid cyst over the described lipoma and trichilemmal-cyst differentials.
claims.limitation: Sole direct descriptive source, section 4. Not an absolute diagnostic exclusion rule: the case supplies a punctum-bearing lesion, and the learner selects the best fit rather than confirming pathology.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults comparing proposed diagnoses for a supplied cutaneous lump.

claims.statement: A skin cyst can become inflamed and painful, so tenderness alone does not define every cyst as an abscess.
claims.limitation: Sources support possible inflammation; the cases supply no redness, tenderness or draining collection. No infection probability, antibiotic indication or drainage/excision protocol is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a supplied noninflamed punctum-bearing lump.

claims.statement: A blood clot within an external hemorrhoid produces a thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
claims.limitation: Sole direct clot-definition source is undated public ASCRS education, not a formal management guideline. No fixed symptom window or automatic excision recommendation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with an examined clot-filled external anal-margin lump.

claims.statement: External hemorrhoids can present as a tender, painful lump at the anal margin.
claims.limitation: Independent specialist/government recognition sources. NIDDK review date is 2016. Pain is nonspecific; supplied examination shows the external clot and excludes a visible tear or draining collection.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with an acutely painful external anal-margin lump.

claims.statement: Internal hemorrhoids arise within the anal canal and may protrude through the anus.
claims.limitation: Anatomic distinction only. Internal prolapse can also hurt; pain alone does not distinguish internal and external disease. The cases explicitly locate the clot under external anal skin, without protruding mucosal tissue.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults distinguishing a supplied external lesion from internal prolapse.

claims.statement: Anal symptoms require assessment rather than automatic attribution to hemorrhoids.
claims.limitation: Sources emphasize other possible causes. The draft supplies an examination, not a rule to diagnose from a patient's complaint or to ignore bleeding. No treatment decision is tested.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with anal pain or a perianal lump.

claims.statement: Repeated vigorous cleansing can irritate perianal skin and worsen anal itching.
claims.limitation: Society/government patient guidance; not a diagnostic accuracy claim or proof of the cause in every person. Cases supply examination and irritant exposure, without a focal lesion requiring different care.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with assessed perianal irritation and excessive cleansing.

claims.statement: Gentle water cleansing followed by patting the area dry is an appropriate basic skin-care measure for pruritus ani.
claims.limitation: Two independent guidance sources, but neither a current formal management guideline. Limited to assessed uncomplicated irritation; no medication, prescribed device or guaranteed response is claimed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with assessed uncomplicated anal itching.

claims.statement: Avoiding fragranced products and abrasive cleaning helps reduce perianal irritation.
claims.limitation: Sources agree on avoiding irritation. ASCRS mentions some gentle wiping options; this is not interpreted as endorsing fragranced wipes. No blanket claim that every wipe or every cleanser is harmful.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with perianal itching while using irritating products.

claims.statement: Persistent or otherwise concerning anal itching warrants reassessment for an underlying cause.
claims.limitation: No fixed follow-up interval or red-flag algorithm is authored. The initial skin-care choice is not a substitute for examining a lesion or reassessing ongoing symptoms.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults receiving basic skin-care counseling for anal itching.

claims.statement: Colonoscopy with inadequate cleansing may fail to assess the colonic lining adequately.
claims.limitation: Official ESGE guideline plus directly read 2025 society summary; the latter is not the full USMSTF guideline. Cases specify inadequate assessment throughout the colon after attempted cleaning, excluding the partial-distal-examination exception.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults reviewing a colonoscopy that cannot support a standard screening assessment.

claims.statement: An inadequately prepared colonoscopy that cannot support the intended assessment should be repeated with adequate preparation.
claims.limitation: Current society summary corroborates guideline direction. No universal numerical interval or mandatory same/next-day schedule; timing, contraindications and urgency require the treating team's assessment. Alternative screening proposals do not complete the inadequate examination in these cases.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults suitable for repeat colonoscopy after an entirely inadequate screening examination.

claims.statement: Reviewing why preparation failed can guide improved instructions and an individualized repeat-preparation plan.
claims.limitation: Source-supported planning only. No specific laxative formulation, dose, diet duration, split-dose timetable or contraindication protocol is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults planning repeat colonoscopy after inadequate bowel cleansing.

claims.statement: Cold snare is the preferred removal technique for an accessible diminutive nonpedunculated colorectal polyp without invasive features.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate directly read guideline, ESGE 2024 section 7.1, strong recommendation/high-quality evidence for polyps at most 5 mm; the synthetic example is 4 mm. No technique algorithm, margin width, risk estimate or difficult-access exception is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a supplied accessible 4 mm nonpedunculated colorectal polyp selected for removal.

claims.statement: Cold snare is the preferred removal technique for a small nonpedunculated colorectal polyp without invasive features.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate directly read guideline, ESGE 2024 section 7.2, strong recommendation/high-quality evidence for 6-9 mm polyps; the example is 7 mm. Excludes pedunculated, invasive-appearing and complex lesions and medication-specific planning.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a supplied accessible 7 mm nonpedunculated colorectal polyp selected for removal.

claims.statement: Cold forceps are not the preferred excision method for the supplied 4 mm or 7 mm polyps because complete resection is less reliable.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate guideline, sections 7.1/7.2 and recommendation against routine cold-forceps excision. Very tiny or difficult-access exceptions are outside these cases; no numerical recurrence estimate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults comparing techniques for the supplied accessible 4 mm or 7 mm lesions.

claims.statement: Hot biopsy forceps are discouraged for diminutive colorectal-polyp excision because of resection, specimen and thermal-injury concerns.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate direct guideline, section 7.1, strong/high-quality recommendation. No exact risk estimate or categorical prohibition on all electrosurgical techniques. For the 7 mm case, the cold-snare preference supplies the direct rejection basis.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults comparing forceps and snare plans for the supplied small lesions.

claims.statement: Endoscopic surveillance is an appropriate follow-up strategy for established nondysplastic Barrett esophagus in a suitable patient.
claims.limitation: Official ESGE guideline plus independent current government surveillance explanation. Cases supply established segments, no dysplasia/visible lesion and suitability for follow-up/treatment. No interval, zero-risk claim or prophylactic surgery indication.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with established nondysplastic Barrett who are suitable for surveillance.

claims.statement: Prophylactic endoscopic ablation is not recommended for Barrett esophagus without dysplasia.
claims.limitation: Sole direct guideline for this negative recommendation; NIDDK only corroborates surveillance. This is not applied to confirmed dysplasia or cancer. No promise that Barrett has no cancer risk.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed nondysplastic Barrett and no visible neoplastic lesion.

claims.statement: Barrett surveillance planning depends on the established segment and the patient's suitability for surveillance and possible treatment.
claims.limitation: Do not extrapolate to an irregular Z-line, limited life expectancy, confirmed dysplasia or visible neoplasia. All numerical surveillance/cessation schedules are withheld in this batch.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults planning follow-up for established nondysplastic Barrett.

claims.statement: A patient receiving endoscopic sedation should arrange transport home rather than plan to drive immediately afterward.
claims.limitation: Current gastroscopy-specific NHS advice and independent NIDDK colonoscopy transport boundary. Cases use planned gastroscopy with sedation. No universal elapsed-time clearance or substitution for formal discharge criteria.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults arranging discharge after planned sedated gastroscopy.

claims.statement: A responsible adult should collect and support the patient after gastroscopy with sedation.
claims.limitation: Sole direct source for collection plus ongoing adult support is the current trust leaflet. Government colonoscopy advice corroborates the ride, not this entire support arrangement. Local discharge policy and clinical readiness remain separate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults preparing for gastroscopy with sedation and an available responsible adult.

claims.statement: Sedation can affect judgment and reactions despite the patient feeling awake after the procedure.
claims.limitation: Sole direct current gastroscopy discharge source. Subjective wakefulness is not driving clearance; no duration, test score or claim that adult accompaniment alone establishes discharge fitness.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults discussing travel after gastroscopy with sedation.

claims.statement: A penicillin-allergy label does not by itself confirm an immune-mediated penicillin reaction.
claims.limitation: Current CDC guidance and eligible perioperative review. Labels can reflect incomplete or nonallergic histories; this does not mean every label is false or authorize automatic removal. No prevalence or cross-reactivity percentage.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with an incompletely characterized penicillin-allergy entry before ASC care.

claims.statement: Characterizing the original drug, reaction symptoms, timing, severity and subsequent exposures is an initial step in evaluating a penicillin-allergy label.
claims.limitation: Current CDC clinical questions plus perioperative history/risk-assessment discussion. The draft asks for history first, without choosing a prophylactic drug, skin-test protocol or oral-challenge procedure.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults whose preoperative allergy record lacks a detailed reaction history.

claims.statement: Reaction history and risk assessment should guide whether further penicillin-allergy testing or referral is appropriate.
claims.limitation: Not everyone is eligible for the same testing pathway, and severe delayed reactions require a different approach. No unsupervised challenge, universal skin testing, automatic delabeling or cefazolin-selection rule is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing assessment of an uncertain preoperative penicillin label.

claims.statement: Surgical-site hair need not be removed when it does not interfere with the operation.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate direct guideline, essential-practices section 4.5. Acute-care hospital recommendation applied to a supplied non-genital ambulatory preparation plan; clinician review of that application is required. No routine-removal benefit or exact SSI probability is claimed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults preparing for a non-genital ambulatory procedure with noninterfering hair.

claims.statement: When surgical-site hair must be removed, clippers are an appropriate method for the supplied non-genital operative field.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate guideline, section 4.5. Depilatory agents are another guideline option and are not presented as incorrect when removal is needed. Clippers are available in the case; no precise preparation timetable, device protocol or genital-field extrapolation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with hair interfering with preparation of a non-genital ambulatory operative field.

claims.statement: A depilatory agent is another guideline-supported option when surgical-site hair removal is needed.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate guideline, section 4.5. This acknowledges an alternative rather than prescribing a formulation or declaring every product appropriate. No depilatory is required when hair does not interfere; non-genital fields only.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults discussing necessary non-genital surgical-site hair removal.

claims.statement: Razor shaving is avoided for routine hair preparation of the supplied non-genital surgical field.
claims.limitation: Sole adequate guideline. The guideline includes a genital/scrotal exception; those operations are explicitly outside this objective. No universal statement about every procedure or exact infection-risk multiplier.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults comparing preparation plans for a non-genital operative field.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 42-year-old woman, visits the clinic after finding rust-coloured spots inside the left side of the bra between examinations. During the visit, compression produces pale fluid from several openings on each nipple; a reddish drop is also seen at one left-sided opening.
before.Task: Which interpretation best accounts for Jamie Taylor's nipple-discharge history?
Options: **KEY:** Pathologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Physiologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Endocrine-mediated left-sided episodes; endocrine-mediated expressed secretion

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 42-year-old woman, visits the clinic after finding rust-coloured spots inside the left side of the bra between examinations. During the visit, compression produces pale fluid from several openings on each nipple; a reddish drop is also seen at one left-sided opening.
after.Task: How should Jamie Taylor's left-sided staining between visits be interpreted?

before: **KEY:** Pathologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Distinguishes the unilateral staining episodes from the bilateral secretion elicited during examination; one pattern need not explain every observation.
Physiologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Overweights the bilateral expressed fluid and treats the separate left-sided history as reassuring.
Endocrine-mediated left-sided episodes; endocrine-mediated expressed secretion
Attributes the combined history to a systemic endocrine explanation because pale fluid can be expressed from both breasts, underweighting the focal reddish episodes.
after: **KEY:** Pathologic nipple discharge
Treats the separate unprovoked unilateral reddish episodes as a pathologic discharge pattern despite the bilateral expressed secretion.
Physiologic nipple discharge
Overweights the bilateral expressed fluid and treats the separate left-sided history as reassuring.
Galactorrhea
Attributes the combined history to a systemic endocrine explanation because pale fluid can be expressed from both breasts, underweighting the focal reddish episodes.

pilotPacket.inference: Classify the focal between-visit episodes while distinguishing them from the secretion produced during examination.
pilotPacket.focus: Three conventional discharge interpretations replace compound paired statements. Confirm the episode-specific task keeps the categories sufficiently distinct and galactorrhea is a credible distractor; no lesion diagnosis is inferred.
pilotPacket.whatChanged: Replace the awkward paired-pattern answer statements with three short, natural clinical interpretations. Focus the task on the left-sided episodes; the mixed raw observations remain as competing evidence.

before.message: Labels overlap substantially; small differences can be meaningful and need review.

evidence.text: Pathologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion

before: **KEY:** Achalasia
A separate per-choice rationale was not supplied; needs clinician review.
Distal esophageal spasm
The reported pattern is absent peristalsis with impaired junction relaxation rather than premature contractions.
Reflux-related dysmotility
The combined manometric findings more directly support achalasia.
Rumination syndrome
Rumination does not produce this esophageal manometric pattern.
after: **KEY:** Achalasia
Integrates failed propagation with the abnormal junction-relaxation measurement rather than relying on either finding alone.
Esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction
Overweights the elevated relaxation pressure; this competing category retains evidence of peristalsis rather than the supplied universally failed propagation.
Absent contractility
Overweights the failed contractions; this category requires a normal relaxation-pressure measurement rather than the supplied elevated value.

batchPacket.inference: Integrate the relaxation measurement and propagated-contraction observations to distinguish neighboring manometric categories.

before: **KEY:** A 40% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
The 0.40 is the probability of data this extreme or more under the specified null model and its analysis assumptions. A larger number retains the same conditioning.
A 40% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
A p-value does not estimate the probability that the null is true. The 0.40 concerns data calculated assuming the null model.
A 60% probability that no group difference exists after observing these results
Subtracting p from one gives 0.60 arithmetically, but does not make that the probability of no effect.
An estimated difference of 0.40 outcome units between the two groups being compared
A probability under the null model is not a 0.40-unit outcome difference. Effect magnitude requires its own estimate.
after: **KEY:** A 40% probability of data at least this extreme if the null model holds
Conditions on the stated null model and its assumptions when interpreting the tail probability.
A 40% probability that the null model holds after these data are observed
Reverses the conditional relationship and treats the p-value as a posterior probability of the hypothesis.
A 40% reduction in outcome probability for the intervention compared with the control
Mistakes the p-value for a treatment effect on the outcome probability.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the emergency-surgery journal-club lead, reviews a new anastomosis instrument after ileal resection for symptomatic Meckel diverticulum. The trial records leak within thirty days. Its analysis does not reject the prespecified null model, and a draft conclusion says the instruments have exactly equal effects. The report gives the p-value and that proposed conclusion for the team's discussion.

Exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational Meckel resection anastomosis instrument trial: invented analysis of thirty-day leak for practice. The null specifies no group difference; the p-value is not an effect size or personal outcome probability.

before.Task: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for thirty-day leak in the constructed trial?
Options: **KEY:** The result does not prove exact equality
The result favors equal group effects
The result indicates a small clinical difference
The result gives an 8% probability of no effect

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the journal-club lead, reviews a report comparing two investigational anastomosis instruments after ileal resection. The constructed trial records leak within thirty days.

Exhibit.caption: Fictional teaching dataset; intervention effects are simulated. Comparison of leak outcomes; null hypothesis: equal event probabilities.

after.Task: Which conclusion should Jamie Taylor include in the trial report?
Options: **KEY:** The data leave clinical importance unresolved
The data favor clinically equivalent outcomes
The data favor a clinically small treatment effect

before: **KEY:** The result does not prove exact equality
The p-value does not prove a zero group difference. The exact-equality sentence claims more than the reported probability establishes.
The result favors equal group effects
Failure to establish a difference is not proof or a supplied probability of equality. The p-value alone does not settle whether the means are exactly equal.
The result indicates a small clinical difference
The exhibit supplies no effect magnitude or clinical-importance criterion. A p-value alone cannot establish a small clinical difference.
The result gives an 8% probability of no effect
The 0.08 describes data conditional on a null model, not an 8% probability that no effect exists after observing the data.
after: **KEY:** The data leave clinical importance unresolved
Does not infer equivalence or clinical effect size from the reported p-value.
The data favor clinically equivalent outcomes
Treats failure to establish a difference as evidence favoring equivalence.
The data favor a clinically small treatment effect
Treats the p-value as evidence favoring a small effect rather than recognizing that effect size and uncertainty were not supplied.

batchPacket.inference: Choose a defensible report conclusion without turning a p-value into equivalence or an effect-size bound.
batchPacket.focus: The fictional 0.08 is unchanged. No unreported significance threshold or equivalence margin is assumed.
batchPacket.whatChanged: Remove the pre-answer non-rejection interpretation, exact-equality draft and effect-size teaching. Compare three natural report conclusions of similar length.

before: **KEY:** Abandon this version and test another idea

Adapt the pathway labels and repeat this version

The tested version missed the aim and increased care-planning time, so the evidence does not support adopting it while monitoring later.

Links repeated lack of benefit and added burden to a different next test rather than rollout or unchanged repetition.

Repeats the unsuccessful design without a stated reason that would address the repeated findings.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the groin-surgery research lead, reviews a new reinforcement material for femoral hernia repair. The trial reports recurrence within two years as a risk ratio with an interval. The sponsor welcomes uncertainty in principle, but asks whether it can be moved to the appendix. The team is reviewing how the reported range relates to the no-difference value.

Exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational femoral-hernia reinforcement material: invented two-year recurrence risk ratio, unitless ratio (new/control), for practice. No real efficacy or clinical-importance threshold.

before.Task: How does the constructed two-year recurrence risk-ratio interval relate to its null value, and what interpretation is justified?
Options: **KEY:** The interval includes the null value 1
The interval excludes the null value 1
The interval gives 95% probability of a real association
The interval supports an exactly absent association

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the study discussion lead, reviews an investigational femoral-hernia reinforcement study. The constructed trial compares recurrence over two years.

Exhibit.caption: Fictional teaching dataset; intervention effects are simulated. Intervention versus control recurrence.

after.Task: Which summary should Jamie Taylor use for the recurrence estimate?
Options: **KEY:** Recurrence could be 60% lower or 20% higher
Recurrence could be 40% lower or 120% higher
Recurrence could be 30% lower or 70% higher

before: **KEY:** The interval includes the null value 1
One lies between 0.40 and 1.20, so the interval includes the no-association value for a ratio. Inclusion does not establish an exactly true ratio of one.
The interval excludes the null value 1
The upper limit is 1.20 and the lower limit is 0.40. One is inside these limits, so it is not excluded.
The interval gives 95% probability of a real association
The 95% level describes coverage of the interval method. It does not give a 95% probability that an association is real.
The interval supports an exactly absent association
An interval containing one is compatible with the ratio null value, but also contains other ratios. It does not prove that the association is exactly absent.
after: **KEY:** Recurrence could be 60% lower or 20% higher
Converts the existing ratio bounds: 0.40 corresponds to 60% lower relative risk, and 1.20 to 20% higher relative risk, while retaining uncertainty.
Recurrence could be 40% lower or 120% higher
Mistakes the ratio endpoints for percentage decreases and increases instead of comparing each endpoint with one.
Recurrence could be 30% lower or 70% higher
Mixes the point estimate's relative reduction with the point estimate itself rather than interpreting the interval endpoints.

batchPacket.inference: Translate both ratio endpoints into relative differences and recognize that the interval spans lower and higher recurrence.
batchPacket.focus: The original 0.70 estimate and 0.40 to 1.20 interval remain. The new percentages are derived arithmetic, not invented clinical probabilities. Confirm the frequentist compatibility language; no clinical-importance threshold is supplied.
batchPacket.whatChanged: Remove sponsor prose, null-value teaching and the uniquely hedged key. All three options now use the same could-be form and numerical scale; the resident must interpret both existing interval endpoints.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the gastric-oncology discussion lead, reviews a new agent for gastric MALT lymphoma in an invented recurrence-prevention trial after remission. Follow-up lasts two years. The sponsor requests 'life-changing' on every slide, including the Wi-Fi password. The trial reports a very small p-value, with its effect estimate supplied separately; the team is reviewing the interpretation for its report.

Exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational gastric-MALT agent trial: invented analysis of two-year lymphoma recurrence for practice. The null specifies no group difference; the p-value is not an effect size or personal outcome probability.

before.Task: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for two-year lymphoma recurrence in the constructed trial?
Options: **KEY:** A 0.1% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
A 0.1% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
A 99.9% probability that the intervention truly changed the outcome after observing these results
An estimated difference of 0.001 outcome units between the two groups being compared

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, the journal-club lead, reviews an investigational gastric-MALT recurrence prevention study. It compares an intervention with a control and reports recurrence within two years.

Exhibit.caption: Fictional teaching dataset; intervention effects are simulated. Null hypothesis: equal outcome probabilities in the two groups.

items.label: Analysis
items.value: Prespecified comparison of intervention and control

after.Task: Which interpretation of the reported p-value should Jamie Taylor use?
Options: **KEY:** A 0.1% probability of data at least this extreme if the null model holds
A 0.1% probability that the null model holds after these data are observed
A 0.1% reduction in outcome probability for the intervention compared with the control

before: **KEY:** A 0.1% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
Under the specified null model and conditions, data this incompatible or more have probability 0.001. The small value does not change what the probability describes.
A 0.1% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
The test assumes the null model when calculating this probability; it does not assign 0.001 probability to the null hypothesis itself.
A 99.9% probability that the intervention truly changed the outcome after observing these results
The complement 0.999 is not a posterior probability that an effect is true. That interpretation does not follow from the reported p-value.
An estimated difference of 0.001 outcome units between the two groups being compared
The number 0.001 is a probability, not an effect in outcome units. The exhibit says the effect estimate is reported separately.
after: **KEY:** A 0.1% probability of data at least this extreme if the null model holds
Conditions on the stated null model and its assumptions when interpreting the tail probability.
A 0.1% probability that the null model holds after these data are observed
Reverses the conditional relationship and treats the p-value as a posterior probability of the hypothesis.
A 0.1% reduction in outcome probability for the intervention compared with the control
Mistakes the p-value for a treatment effect on the outcome probability.

batchPacket.inference: Translate the reported p-value into its null-conditional meaning while distinguishing posterior belief and effect size.
batchPacket.focus: The supplied numerical values are retained from the fictional trial, not clinical probabilities. Check statistical assumptions and parallel option meanings; no personal benefit claim is made.

Bipolar coagulation alone
Contact thermal therapy is an accepted monotherapy for a nonbleeding visible vessel.
Endoscopic clip alone
Mechanical clip therapy is an accepted monotherapy for a nonbleeding visible vessel.

adversarialReview.title: HIDA after equivocal gallbladder ultrasound
fairness: No strong nonmedical wording cue: the ultrasound components are observations, not the label 'equivocal'. Interpretation followed by selection of a functional study is genuinely two-step.

Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is defensible, but CT and biliary MRI can also be defensible after nondiagnostic ultrasound depending on the clinical question. The stem does not clearly distinguish persistent concern for cystic-duct obstruction from alternative abdominal pathology or ductal disease. I cannot certify a unique next-test ranking from these fields alone.

The sonographic Murphy assessment and biliary-duct findings are not supplied; whether either changes the intended ranking needs clinician review. Do not invent their results merely to eliminate choices.
suggestions: Have Melissa specify the narrow unresolved question and confirm the next-test ranking against the exact option set; retain the raw ultrasound observations.

Define 'Biliary magnetic resonance imaging' consistently, including whether it means MRI with MRCP. If multiple modalities remain defensible, change the task to the clinical property being assessed or select closer but unambiguously inferior alternatives.
Do not restore 'inconclusive' or add a sentence announcing that HIDA is needed.

adversarialReview.title: Classify nipple discharge patterns

cues.why: A lay reader can associate rusty/red spontaneous staining with 'pathologic', especially against physiologic and milk-related labels. This is a weak everyday-language cue, not a reason to remove clinically essential blood-colour observations.

One specific secretion syndrome is contrasted with two broad evaluative categories; the taxonomy and one-word length differ. Galactorrhea can overlap physiologic discharge, so these are not parallel competing categories.

fairness: Spontaneous unilateral staining supports the key despite expressed bilateral multiduct fluid; the coexisting patterns are a useful distraction.
The task explicitly selects the concerning component, so the learner need not resolve the mixed findings. This is recognition, likely too easy for a routine PGY-2/3 item.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the category overlap does not make galactorrhea a credible explanation of the specified staining.
suggestions: Keep the mixed raw observations but ask for a consequential evaluation decision that requires interpreting both patterns.

If classification is the objective, label it foundational and use three genuinely competing interpretations at the same level of specificity. Do not make the stem less informative simply to increase difficulty.

adversarialReview.title: Select diagnostic imaging for pathologic discharge

cues.why: Only the key combines two tests and explicitly labels mammography diagnostic. A symptomatic patient makes 'diagnostic' versus 'screening' a low-knowledge shortcut; the bundled workup looks more complete than each single-test alternative.

cues.phrase: The left-sided staining has continued between visits.
cues.why: Repeats the spontaneous interval-staining signal already present in the presentation and makes reassessment alone an especially weak competitor.

fairness: At the supplied age and with spontaneous unilateral blood-coloured staining, diagnostic mammography with ultrasound is defensible as an initial evaluation.
Two steps are available: classify the concerning discharge component, then select an age-appropriate diagnostic workup. The current option packaging makes both straightforward.
No prior breast imaging is supplied; the item should establish initial evaluation so MRI is not interpreted as a subsequent-workup alternative. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: State the stage of evaluation without naming the preferred modality.
Use parallel diagnostic pathways rather than a two-test diagnostic bundle against screening, one advanced test and waiting.
Retain spontaneous staining as necessary information, but remove a redundant update unless persistence materially changes the decision.

adversarialReview.title: Perioperative ART continuity
fairness: No reliable key-only lexical or length cue; 'complete prescribed regimen' occurs in both continuation and interruption choices.

Continuation is a defensible default for an uncomplicated elective operation. Naming the regimen alone does not make the task require recognition of an interaction; the answer can be recalled without using its components.

Oral dosing feasibility and the planned perioperative medications are unspecified. These omissions do not by themselves prove the key wrong, but prevent this from being an individualized interaction/continuity decision.
suggestions: Make the medication list consequential: supply one verified planned perioperative medication or a concrete oral-access issue, then offer parallel complete plans that handle that issue and ART continuity.
Alternatively retain as an explicitly foundational continuity item. Do not introduce an arbitrary interruption interval or drug-management rule without clinician verification.

adversarialReview.title: Boosted ART and midazolam

cues.why: The key is broadly flexible rather than a concrete prescription; it can encompass almost any safe adjustment, while the alternatives commit to specific errors.
No inadequate sedation is described, making dose escalation an unmotivated distractor even without knowing the interaction.

fairness: Recognizing the boosted regimen and applying the route-specific sedation interaction is genuinely two-step and potentially moderate for residents.
The oral route matters and is supplied. Revising the sedation plan is defensible, but too vague to show whether the learner knows what change is needed.

Withholding ART is not a well-specified alternative: timing is absent, and a learner should not infer immediate disappearance of interaction effects. Exact pharmacologic handling remains for clinician verification; none is asserted here.
suggestions: Offer three concrete, comparably detailed medication-coordination plans, all preserving necessary procedural support.
Retain the exact medication names and oral route; do not add a sentence naming the metabolic interaction.
Replace unexplained dose escalation with a realistic misconception, and have Melissa verify every proposed drug/route combination.

adversarialReview.title: Manometric recognition of achalasia

cues.why: The key is a one-word diagnosis between a four-word and a two-word diagnosis. This is only a weak shortest-label heuristic; terminology should not be padded to equalize it.

fairness: The elevated relaxation pressure plus absent propagated contractions favors achalasia over the two offered neighboring diagnoses. No strong nonmedical cue chooses it; the manometric distinction requires knowledge.
This is direct recognition of the defining pair of findings, not two-step reasoning. Likely too easy for PGY-2/3 residents familiar with foregut physiology.

The absence of a fixed narrowing or intraluminal mass is legitimate workup context, not an option-specific exclusion of either motility distractor. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this is not a subtype-classification task.
suggestions: Either label this a foundational interpretation item or test a subsequent clinically consequential decision after the resident interprets the tracing.
For a harder interpretation item, use clinician-verified discordant or borderline raw findings with enough data to distinguish the offered diagnoses; do not fabricate thresholds.
Across B01-B04, vary a meaningful diagnostic distinction rather than just age and paraphrases of the same manometric pair.

adversarialReview.title: High-resolution manometry for suspected achalasia

cues.phrase: Endoscopy shows no fixed narrowing or intraluminal mass.
cues.why: Paired with 'Repeat upper-GI endoscopy', the reported negative examination makes that choice look redundant without an explicit reason to repeat it. This narrows the set by ordinary sequencing logic, although it does not alone identify manometry.

fairness: Inferring a motility problem from mixed solid/liquid dysphagia and then selecting manometry is a legitimate two-step chain.

Manometry is a defensible next investigation among these choices after the reported endoscopy. The absence of a mass is appropriate workup context and must not be removed simply to preserve a repeat-endoscopy distractor.
The repeated endoscopy and chest CT alternatives are weak without a new structural concern. Likely easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Normal-appearing endoscopy alone should not be represented as excluding every possible mechanical or secondary cause.
suggestions: Replace the unmotivated repeat endoscopy with a credible same-stage test, such as a clinician-reviewed contrast-swallow strategy, and specify the unresolved question sufficiently to rank it against manometry.
Keep the actual endoscopic findings and symptom pattern; avoid the interpretive label 'motility disorder'.
Vary relevant workup details across siblings instead of only names, ages and symptom paraphrases.

adversarialReview.title: Dynamic ultrasound after an equivocal inguinal-hernia examination
fairness: No strong nonmedical wording cue. Positional/intermittent swelling plus a nonreproducing examination supports an occult/reducible hernia inference followed by initial imaging selection.

Ultrasound is a defensible initial study, but MRI is a legitimate diagnostic alternative in some occult-hernia pathways. The task does not explicitly establish that this is the first imaging assessment; clinician confirmation of the intended ranking is needed.
The broad modality labels do not specify a dynamic assessment. The item is likely easy for PGY-2/3 residents despite its simple two-step structure.
suggestions: Specify that no prior groin imaging has been performed if true, and use comparable protocol-level labels for all modalities, including the intended dynamic ultrasound examination.

To test a resident-level decision, supply a verified prior study with persistent discordant findings and ask what resolves that uncertainty, rather than adding availability language that hands over the answer.
Differentiate these four variants by clinically meaningful workup or findings, not merely the activity provoking swelling.

adversarialReview.title: Elective planning for symptomatic inguinal hernia

cues.why: The task supplies both the diagnosis and its symptom status; 'Elective hernia repair consultation' is the only option naming hernia treatment.

cues.phrase: Physical therapy for presumed groin strain
cues.why: The word 'presumed' plus a different diagnosis is self-undermining after explicit ultrasound confirmation of a hernia.
A reducible hernia with activity limitation but no acute complication makes the emergency option conspicuously mismatched.

fairness: An elective repair discussion is defensible for activity-limiting symptoms in a confirmed reducible hernia; consultation appropriately leaves shared decision-making open.
The activity-impact detail is necessary patient context, not an unfair preference to be deleted.

The update already supplies the interpretation, so this is one-step management selection and likely too easy for residents. Observation remains a real option for selected patients but is reasonably less favored in the stated symptomatic scenario.
suggestions: Keep confirmation and functional impact, but replace the groin-strain and emergency fillers with credible management discussions for the same known condition.
If the target is ordinary symptomatic-hernia referral, label it foundational.
For a harder item, introduce a verified competing operative-risk or timing consideration and give enough information to distinguish the plans; do not hide a necessary patient goal.

adversarialReview.title: Map DTC with preoperative neck ultrasound
fairness: No reliable answer-from-wording cue: 'neck' occurs in both ultrasound and CT labels.

Neck ultrasound is a defensible mapping study, but prior FNA commonly follows some thyroid imaging; the stem does not say whether complete nodal mapping has already occurred. CT could be reasonable depending on the extent and location of disease.
Known papillary carcinoma plus a palpable node prompts a familiar preoperative study, making this one-step and likely too easy for the target audience.
suggestions: Clarify the scope of existing imaging, not just the existence of FNA, and what information is missing before surgery.
For a harder item, provide a raw nodal imaging finding and ask for the next diagnostic/staging action with clinically credible alternatives; verify the exact biopsy criteria before adding them.

adversarialReview.title: Escalate complicated stoma prolapse

cues.why: Together with vomiting and reduced output, the irreducibility language lets a general reader choose the most urgent of three urgency labels. It is necessary safety information, so the problem is the simplistic option set, not the finding itself.
Routine follow-up is conspicuously mismatched to the supplied acute obstructive symptoms and adds little competition.

fairness: Emergency surgical assessment is the defensible disposition for the described concerning presentation.
Recognition of a complicated prolapse followed by escalation is two-step but very straightforward; likely too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
Red, swollen bowel alone does not establish ischemia. The key is assessment, so the item need not claim proven ischemia.
suggestions: Retain the vomiting, reduced output and irreducibility; never remove red flags to make an urgent scenario harder.
Use as an explicitly foundational safety/disposition item, or test a more discriminating next action after escalation using clinician-verified findings and realistic alternatives.

adversarialReview.title: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma

cues.phrase: No enlarged nodes are felt in the draining basin.
cues.why: This exact negative appears twice. It repeatedly steers away from complete nodal dissection. One occurrence is necessary staging context; duplication overemphasizes the exclusion.
With a clinically negative basin stated twice, this aggressive alternative makes biopsy versus surveillance the only credible contest.

fairness: The supplied invasive melanoma thickness and clinically negative basin support the sentinel-node option in the ordinary patient represented here.
This is direct application of a familiar staging rule, not a substantive two-step inference; likely too easy for routine PGY-2/3 difficulty.
No confident inaccuracy identified. The clinical description 'small and superficial' should not be treated as histologic depth; the actual thickness is supplied separately.
suggestions: Keep one nodal examination statement and remove its duplicate.

If retaining the simple staging rule, label the item foundational. To raise difficulty, introduce a verified decision-relevant pathology or patient constraint and recheck every offered plan rather than shifting the number slightly.
Make variants differ in a clinically meaningful staging decision; the current thickness changes preserve the same easy rule.

adversarialReview.title: Complete diagnostic biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion

cues.why: 'Complete' sounds preferable to the explicitly 'Partial' and 'Superficial' diagnostic alternatives; the key is the only biopsy label without a limitation built into its adjective.
The partial qualifier advertises incomplete sampling, letting test-wise readers reject it without understanding microstaging.
'Definitive' answers a later treatment question rather than the requested biopsy approach, creating a stage/category mismatch.

fairness: Recognizing a suspicious pigmented lesion then selecting complete diagnostic sampling is a simple two-step sequence, likely easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
Complete excisional biopsy is defensible for the small accessible lesion described. The partial and superficial options could be relevant in other circumstances, but none is supplied here.
The normal nodal examination does not select the diagnostic skin-biopsy method and may be dispensable at this stage.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; 'superficial shave' should not be generalized to all tangential/deep saucerization techniques.
suggestions: Use comparable procedural descriptions without value-laden complete/partial contrasts, while retaining enough information about depth and sampling extent to assess the actual techniques.
If testing a biopsy exception, provide a real supported anatomic/size constraint; otherwise label the routine approach foundational.
Keep definitive therapy separate from the diagnostic-biopsy option set unless wrong-stage care is a meaningful resident-level misconception.

adversarialReview.title: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer

cues.why: The key is the compromise between 'Local full-thickness excision of the tumour' and 'Total abdominal colectomy with lymphadenectomy'. A least-versus-most-versus-middle heuristic weakly favors it without knowing oncologic principles.

fairness: Regional oncologic resection is a defensible best answer for the localized invasive lesion described; imaging-negative nodes do not establish absence of microscopic nodal disease.

suggestions: Provide a constructed effect estimate and interval plus a clearly stated clinical question; compare conclusions of similar certainty and specificity.

adversarialReview.title: Act and iterate after a PDSA test

cues.phrase: Successive tests miss the symptom target and take longer to plan care.
cues.why: The intervention is presented as failing on every reported dimension, so ordinary common sense selects change rather than continuation or expansion.

cues.phrase: An audit finds staff followed the tested workflow.
cues.why: This summary forecloses implementation failure without giving audit observations; it plays the same cueing role as 'taken as prescribed'.

cues.phrase: Repeat this version without changing the workflow
cues.why: The negative qualifier makes the distractor sound deliberately unresponsive to the already announced failures.
The exhibit repeats the stem's interpretive adherence conclusion, reinforcing exclusion of another explanation.

fairness: Stopping this version and testing an alternative is reasonable among these choices, but the display lacks observations supporting the strength of the conclusion, including variation or balancing tradeoffs.
PDSA adaptation does not inherently require abandoning an entire approach; 'another approach' could mean a modest revision or a replacement. The intended scope is unclear.
This is a common-sense failure/change decision, likely easy and one-step. The fictional-data label is appropriate.
suggestions: Show a small constructed sequence of observations and actual adherence measures instead of only 'Not met', 'Longer' and 'followed' summaries.
Offer three plausible next tests or adaptations, each responding to a different interpretation of the data, and specify what would discriminate them.
Clarify whether the key means modifying the tested version or abandoning the approach; do not teach an unsupported universal stop rule.

adversarialReview.title: Tissue confirmation of inflammatory breast cancer
fairness: No strong nonmedical key cue. All three options are comparably styled biopsy-plus-staging plans; recognition of the syndrome and choice of tissue target requires knowledge.

Core biopsy of the breast abnormality is defensible for establishing invasive carcinoma. A skin punch can also be part of evaluating suspected inflammatory breast cancer, so the broad 'diagnostic plan' task does not cleanly specify primary tissue confirmation versus an adjunctive biopsy.
All options append staging before the visible record establishes malignancy. This can mean appropriate planning, but should not imply that suspicion alone is histologic confirmation.

The nonlactating status and absence of a fluid pocket are useful context, but neither distinguishes the three biopsy choices. They should undergo the deletion test rather than be counted as direct lexical giveaways.
suggestions: Ask specifically for the initial tissue-sampling step to establish invasive breast carcinoma in the imaged abnormality, while keeping the syndrome inference in the raw presentation.
Offer parallel sampling choices and make clear whether skin sampling is an adjunct or a substitute; have Melissa confirm the one-best distinction.
Separate subsequent staging from tissue diagnosis, or state that it is contingent on confirmation.

adversarialReview.title: Neoadjuvant sequence for stage III inflammatory breast cancer

cues.why: Only the key uses generic 'surgery', while the distractors specify mastectomy or lumpectomy. This breadth avoids committing to an incorrect operation and makes the key structurally safer.
'Then observation' conspicuously omits radiation from the one mastectomy distractor, while the key offers the complete multimodality sequence.
This and the reverse-order lumpectomy option share the same operation and treatments, making two distractors near-duplicates distinguished only by sequencing.

fairness: For the stated confirmed stage III inflammatory breast cancer, a neoadjuvant systemic-treatment, surgery, radiation pathway is defensible.
The diagnosis and stage are supplied, so this is recall of a standard sequence, not two-step reasoning. Likely easy for residents.

The generic 'surgery' wording is underspecified for an item whose alternatives explicitly name operations. Biomarker results need not be stated for this broad sequence, but would be necessary to test a specific systemic regimen.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the broad keyed sequence; clinical review should verify intended surgical eligibility and terminology.
suggestions: Give every option the same level of treatment and operation specificity, and compare clinically credible pathways.
Retain stage and confirmation; if testing a harder decision, provide an actual response or resectability issue and enough information to resolve it.
Do not use two lumpectomy sequences as filler if both fail for the same reason.

adversarialReview.title: Interpret a confidence interval
fairness: No strong lexical, grammar or length cue; all choices are parallel. The key is obtained by converting the two ratio endpoints into relative percentage changes.
The interval supports a range spanning relative benefit and harm under the statistical model; the keyed percentages are arithmetically consistent with 0.40 and 1.20.
'Recurrence could be' omits that these are relative risks and that the endpoints summarize a confidence interval, not hard limits on possible effects. All options share this imprecision.
One direct arithmetic interpretation, likely easy for PGY-2/3 residents; no second decision is required.
suggestions: State 'relative recurrence risk' in each option and use language such as 'the interval ranges from' rather than implying hard bounds on what can occur.

For application-level difficulty, ask what a decision-maker can conclude about benefit/harm given an absolute baseline risk and an explicit clinical decision, with all necessary constructed data supplied.
Retain parallel option grammar.

adversarialReview.title: Interpret a p-value
fairness: No strong nonmedical cue. Option lengths and numeric conversions are comparable; the conditional language is the concept being tested rather than automatically an illegitimate grammar cue.
The key gives the conventional conditional interpretation under the null model. The alternatives reverse the condition or confuse a p-value with an effect size; there is one defensible answer.
This is a memorized definition, not two-step reasoning. Likely too easy for the requested resident-level struggle even if some residents hold the listed misconceptions.
The fabricated data are explicitly labelled. No confidence or causal claim can be derived from the p-value alone.
suggestions: Label as a foundational statistics item, or provide a compact effect estimate, uncertainty interval and study decision that requires applying rather than reciting the definition.
Use the study's clinical endpoint in a real inferential decision instead of attaching a specialty vignette to a generic definition.
Changing only the p-value and disease across B26/B27/B39 does not produce meaningful transfer variants.

adversarialReview.title: High-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata requiring endoscopic hemostasis
fairness: No strong nonmedical cue. The dry field is a useful clinically plausible distraction rather than an explicit exclusion of the keyed therapy.
Recognizing the nonbleeding visible-vessel stigma and selecting endoscopic treatment with acid suppression supports the key; this is a simple two-step chain.
This is a familiar high-risk-stigma rule and likely too easy for routine resident-level struggle. Embolization before any stated endoscopic failure is a weak competitor.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. If prior failed hemostasis or other factors are intended, they must be supplied; none can be assumed.
suggestions: Retain the raw ulcer-base observation and dry field.
Either label as foundational or add a clinically verified treatment-response/history decision that makes the endoscopy-versus-embolization choice consequential.
If testing initial treatment, say so explicitly and compare plausible initial strategies at the same stage of care.

adversarialReview.title: Endoscopic hemostasis modality selection for peptic-ulcer bleeding

cues.why: The task's monotherapy wording immediately excludes the combination option 'Epinephrine plus bipolar coagulation' from the serious contest.

Beside 'Bipolar coagulation alone', this reveals that bipolar is offered as a standalone and combination component; a redundancy/dominance heuristic weakly points to epinephrine alone as the intended inadequate component.

fairness: The presentation identifies a duodenal ulcer after melena, but the update introduces an unnamed adult with maroon stool and a gastric ulcer. These are conflicting patient/lesion contexts, with no explanation that a second lesion or new event has appeared.
The intended epinephrine-monotherapy key is defensible for the stated nonbleeding visible vessel, but that does not repair the inconsistent encounter.
The task is direct recall of a familiar hemostasis rule, likely easy and one-step; the combination option is not a credible answer to which monotherapy should be avoided.
FAIL applies to this assembled draft's internal consistency, not a claim that the intended treatment principle is wrong. Clinical approval is still required.
suggestions: Replace the anonymous gastric-ulcer update with a coherent Jamie-specific update for the same duodenal lesion, or explicitly and consistently change the entire encounter to a gastric lesion.
Use three comparable standalone modalities when asking about sole therapy, or change to an affirmative next-treatment decision after a specified hemostatic attempt.
Re-review the complete allowed presentation/update/task after the consistency repair; do not rely on prior feedback to explain the mismatch.
